questions.title: Sessions across three regions
questions.prompt: An engineering lead presents a design to move user sessions from a single relational database to a distributed cache replicated across three regions. As the TPM for this program, what questions do you ask, and where is the schedule and delivery risk?
hints: What happens to users who are logged in during the cutover?
What if two regions disagree about a session?
How do you roll back if the cache misbehaves at peak?
followups: The team proposes a single big-bang cutover on a weekend. Your view?
Security asks how sessions are revoked everywhere when a password changes. Does that change the plan?
What milestones would you track?
criteria: Asks about consistency, failover and revocation, not only performance.
Identifies migration risk: dual writes or read-through, cutover and rollback.
Turns technical risks into milestones and go/no-go criteria.
Brings in the right dependencies (security, SRE, client teams).
Does not try to redesign the system; asks to understand it.
outline: Purpose: why move (latency, load, regional resilience)? What target?
Data: session size, write rate, time-to-live, revocation needs.
Consistency: what happens on a regional partition; is stale session data acceptable?
Migration: dual-write or read-through period; backfill; percentage rollout by region; rollback path.
Dependencies: security sign-off, SRE runbooks, capacity, client changes.
Milestones: shadow traffic, one region at 5%, all regions, old path removed; go/no-go per step.
questions.reference:
I would first ask why we are moving — latency, database load, or regional resilience — because that sets the success criteria and what we can trade off.

Then the questions that hide schedule risk. Consistency: if regions cannot talk to each other, can a user be logged in one region and logged out in another? Revocation: when someone changes a password or is fired, how fast must every region drop the session? That is a security requirement and may need a different mechanism than replication. Migration: how do existing sessions move — dual writes, read-through from the old database, or forcing everyone to log in again? And rollback: if the cache fails at peak, can we flip back without losing sessions?

I would not accept a big-bang weekend cutover. I would plan shadow traffic first, then one region at a small percentage, then all regions, with a go/no-go at each step based on error rates, latency and revocation tests. Dependencies to bring in early: security for revocation, SRE for runbooks and capacity, client teams if login flows change. My job is not to redesign the cache; it is to make sure these questions have owners and dates.

questions.title: Why the retry made it worse
questions.prompt: During a launch, a downstream service slowed down. Clients retried, traffic tripled, and the whole system fell over. Explain what happened to a non-technical director, and what the program should change before the next launch.
hints: What does a retry do to load on an already-slow service?
What mechanisms stop retries from multiplying?
What launch practices would have limited the damage?
followups: What is a circuit breaker, in plain words?
Who owns fixing this: the client team or the service team?
How do you test this before the next launch?
criteria: Explains cascading failure and retry storms simply.
Names mitigations: backoff with jitter, retry budgets, circuit breakers, load shedding, timeouts.
Adds launch practices: staged rollout, load tests, feature flags.
Assigns ownership across teams.
Plans verification (load or chaos tests).
outline: Plain explanation: slow service → clients wait → time out → retry → more load → slower → everyone retries.
Mitigations: exponential backoff with jitter; retry limits; circuit breakers; load shedding; sensible timeouts.
Launch practice: staged rollout with a kill switch; load test at expected peak × safety margin.
Ownership: shared client library changes; service-side protections; SRE review.
Verification: game day before next launch.
questions.reference:
For the director: the downstream service slowed down, so requests started timing out. Every client then asked again — and again. Each retry added load to a service that was already struggling, so it slowed further and more requests timed out. Within minutes, the retries were most of the traffic. It is like everyone redialling a busy phone line at once.

What changes before the next launch: clients wait progressively longer between retries, with some randomness so they do not retry in sync, and stop after a small number; a circuit breaker stops calling a failing service for a while instead of hammering it; the service sheds load it cannot handle, so it serves some users well instead of all users badly; and timeouts are set deliberately.

Program changes: launches roll out in stages with a kill switch; we load-test at expected peak plus a margin; and we run a failure drill before launch. The client-library change has one owner across teams, the service protections another, and SRE reviews both. I would track these as launch gates, not as nice-to-haves.
pitfalls: No verification before the next launch.

questions.title: Three teams, one immovable date
questions.prompt: Three engineering teams must deliver a shared platform migration. One team is six weeks behind, another has unresolved dependencies, and executive leadership refuses to move the launch date. What would you do?
hints: Why is the date fixed? A contract, a regulation, an event, or a preference?
What is the minimum that must be true at launch?
Which levers exist: scope, people, sequence, risk?
followups: Leadership offers two extra engineers. Will they help?
The lagging team's manager says they will 'catch up'. Do you believe it?
What exactly do you tell executives this week?
criteria: Finds out why the date is fixed and what 'launch' must include.
Re-plans from evidence: critical path, real throughput, dependency status.
Builds options: cut scope, phase the migration, change sequence, add capacity where it actually helps.
Resolves the dependencies with owners and dates.
Brings executives a clear choice with trade-offs, not a hope.
outline: Understand the date: what external fact fixes it; what must be live by then.
Diagnose: why six weeks behind (scope, staffing, unknowns); dependency details.
Re-plan: critical path with real throughput; identify minimum launchable scope.
Options: phased migration (core path first), de-scope, re-sequence, targeted help (people who know the code), parallel work.
Dependencies: named owners, dates, escalation where blocked.
Exec communication: status, options with risk, recommendation, decision needed by date.
questions.reference:
First I would understand why the date cannot move — a customer contract, a regulatory deadline or a marketing event — and what must be true on that day. Often the fixed thing is narrower than ‘the whole migration’.

Then diagnose with evidence. For the lagging team: why six weeks — scope growth, unknowns or staffing — and what their actual throughput says about the remaining work. For the dependencies: what exactly is unresolved, who owns it and what decision is missing. I would rebuild the critical path from that, not from the original plan.

Options usually include: launch the core path on the date and migrate the remaining services in a second phase; cut lower-value scope; re-sequence so the blocked team works on unblocked parts; and add help only where it shortens the critical path — extra engineers rarely speed up a late team in the short term unless they know the code.

I would take executives a one-page decision: current forecast with a range, two or three options with their risks, my recommendation, and the date by which they must choose. ‘We will catch up’ is not an option on that page unless the data supports it.

questions.title: Find the critical path
questions.prompt: Here is the plan for launching a new API. Find the critical path and the earliest launch week, say which tasks have slack, and tell me where you would focus.

table.unit: Durations in weeks. A task can start only when all of its predecessors are finished.

hints: Work forward: each task's earliest finish is its duration plus the latest finish among its predecessors.
There may be more than one critical path.
Slack = how late a task can finish without moving the launch.
followups: The service build (B) slips by a week. What happens to the date?
Could you start the security review earlier?
Where would one extra engineer help most?
criteria: Computes earliest finish times correctly.
Identifies every critical path.
Computes slack for non-critical tasks.
Focuses attention on the critical chain and near-critical tasks.
Proposes ways to shorten the path (parallelise, start reviews early).
outline: Forward pass: earliest start and finish for each task.
Launch week = finish of the last task.
Backward pass: latest finish without moving launch; slack = latest − earliest.
Critical path(s) = tasks with zero slack.
Focus: protect B (on every critical path); start security review on the design; watch near-critical tasks.
questions.reference:
Working forward, the earliest finish of the launch is the end of week 9. The critical paths — tasks with no slack — are A–B–E–H and A–B–F–H. Tasks with slack: C (1 week), D (3 weeks) and G (1 week).

The service build (B) is on every critical path, so any slip in B moves the launch week for week. That is where I would focus: make sure it is staffed with people who know the system, track it weekly with demonstrable milestones, and remove anything that could interrupt it.

To shorten or protect the plan, I would start the security review earlier against the design rather than waiting for the finished service, so G cannot become a surprise; start the backfill tooling (D) immediately since it has no predecessors; and agree the API contract early so the SDK team (C) is never blocked. Near-critical tasks deserve attention too: a task with only a week of slack becomes critical after one bad week.
pitfalls: Adding durations along one chain only.

questions.title: Will we hit the date?
questions.prompt: Your VP asks whether the program will finish in eight weeks. 84 work items remain. Over the last six weeks the team completed 9, 12, 7, 11, 10 and 8 items per week. What do you tell them?
questions.premise: All figures are invented for practice.
hints: What do the slowest, average and fastest weeks imply?
Is the remaining work like the completed work?
Does scope tend to grow during a program?
followups: Scope has grown by about 10% every month so far. Update the forecast.
The VP wants a yes or no. How do you answer?
What would increase throughput without burning out the team?
criteria: Uses historical throughput, not hope.
Gives a range with a confidence level, not a single date.
Accounts for scope growth and differences in remaining work.
Answers the question directly, then explains.
Offers levers to change the outcome.
outline: Average throughput → central estimate; slowest and fastest weeks → range.
Adjust for scope growth and harder remaining work.
Answer: likely, unlikely or at risk; with the range.
Levers: cut scope, remove blockers, re-sequence.
Commit to re-forecast weekly.
questions.reference:
At the average pace of 9.5 items a week, 84 items take about 8.8 weeks. At the fastest week’s pace it would be 7.0 weeks; at the slowest, 12.0. So eight weeks is possible but not the likely outcome — and that is before scope growth.

I would answer directly: “On current evidence, eight weeks is at risk. Our likely finish is around week 9, with a realistic range of 7 to 12 weeks. If scope keeps growing, add more.” Then I would check whether the remaining items are like the completed ones; the hard ones are often left for last.

And I would bring options: which items could move after the date, which blockers are slowing the team, and whether any work can run in parallel. I would re-forecast every week from actual throughput and say what changed. A range with a reason is more useful to a VP than a confident date that slips later.
pitfalls: A single date with false precision.
Saying yes to avoid a hard conversation.

questions.title: A health dashboard for twelve teams
questions.prompt: You are starting an 18-month program across twelve engineering teams. Design the program health dashboard you would review every week, and the thresholds that trigger action.
hints: Which signals show trouble before a milestone is missed?
How do you avoid twelve teams each reporting 'green'?
What about quality and team health, not just dates?
followups: Ten teams are green and the program is late. How is that possible?
Which metric would you remove after three months, and why?
How do you keep teams from gaming the dashboard?
criteria: Uses leading indicators (milestone burn, dependency status, risk trend, scope change).
Includes quality and operational signals.
Includes team health.
Defines thresholds and actions in advance.
Avoids activity metrics and self-reported colours without evidence.
outline: Delivery: milestone completion vs plan (evidence-based), forecast range trend.
Dependencies: count overdue, age of oldest.
Risk: open high risks, new vs retired.
Scope: change since baseline.
Quality: defect trend, test pass rate, error budget.
People: on-call load, attrition risk, overtime signals.
Thresholds: yellow and red per metric with a named action.
questions.reference:
I would review seven signals weekly. Delivery: milestones completed against plan, where ‘complete’ means demonstrated and integrated, not ‘code written’; and the forecast range over time — a range moving right is the earliest warning. Dependencies: the number overdue and the age of the oldest. Risks: open high risks and whether they are being retired. Scope: change since the baseline. Quality: defect trend and error-budget use. People: on-call load and signs of overload.

Each has thresholds agreed with teams at the start — for example, any dependency overdue more than two weeks is red and goes to the weekly review with an owner and a date. Thresholds trigger actions, not just colours.

Ten green teams and a late program usually means the integration work between teams is unowned, or teams report activity rather than evidence. So milestones are cross-team and verified, and I would remove any metric nobody acted on after a quarter.

questions.title: The team that deprioritised you
questions.prompt: Your launch depends on the identity team shipping an API change. They have just moved it out of their quarter to work on a security priority. Your launch is in ten weeks. What do you do?
hints: What exactly do you need from them — the whole change or a part?
Is their security priority more important than your launch? Who decides?
Could your team do some of the work?
followups: The identity team agrees to review your code if your engineers make the change. What risks does that create?
Their director will not discuss it. What next?
How would you have caught this earlier?
criteria: Understands the other team's priority instead of fighting it.
Narrows the ask to the minimum needed.
Proposes options: contributor model, interim workaround, re-sequencing, shared staffing.
Escalates with options to the level that owns both priorities.
Puts a lasting fix in place (dependency agreements, earlier detection).
outline: Meet the identity team lead: understand the security priority and what is left of capacity.
Narrow: smallest API change that unblocks the launch.
Options: our engineers build it, they review; temporary workaround; re-sequence our launch scope.
Escalate if needed to the shared leader with options and impact.
Record the agreement: what, who, when, how verified; watch it weekly.
questions.reference:
I would talk to the identity team lead first, assuming their security priority is legitimate. Then I would narrow my request: often we need one endpoint or one field, not the full change they planned.

Options: our engineers build the change in their codebase with their review (they keep ownership; we supply capacity); a temporary workaround that is safe and reversible; or re-sequencing our launch so the parts that need the identity change come later. If none works, the conflict is between two company priorities — that decision belongs to the leader who owns both, so I would escalate with the options, the impact on each side and my recommendation.

Whatever we agree goes in writing: the exact change, owner, date, how we verify it, and a weekly check. For the future, I would add identity and other shared platforms to the program’s dependency review at the start of each quarter, so a change like this is visible before plans are set.
pitfalls: Treating the other team as the problem.

questions.title: Launching in a new region
questions.prompt: Your company will launch its product in a new country that requires customer data to stay inside its borders. Build the program's risk register: the top risks, how you would size them, and what you would do first.
hints: Which risks are technical, which legal, which operational?
Which unknown would hurt most if discovered late?
How do you retire a risk rather than just monitor it?
followups: Legal's interpretation of the law changes halfway through. How does your plan cope?
Which risk would you spend the first two weeks on?
How often do you review the register, and who attends?
criteria: Covers technical, legal, operational and vendor risks.
Sizes by likelihood and impact.
Assigns owners, mitigations and triggers.
Retires the largest unknowns first with spikes or early decisions.
Builds in contingency and review cadence.
outline: Technical: services that copy data across borders (logs, backups, analytics, support tools); capacity in the new region.
Legal: interpretation of residency rules; certifications needed.
Vendors: third-party tools that store data elsewhere.
Operational: support access from other countries; on-call coverage.
Size: likelihood × impact; owner, mitigation, trigger.
First steps: data-flow inventory (biggest unknown) and legal interpretation in writing.
questions.reference:
The biggest risk is the unknown: data copying itself out of the country through paths nobody remembers — logs, backups, analytics pipelines, support tools, third-party vendors. So the first two weeks go to a data-flow inventory, with engineering leads signing off on each service.

Other top risks: legal interpretation (what counts as ‘inside the borders’ — are encrypted backups abroad allowed? support staff abroad viewing data?); vendor tools with no local hosting; capacity and lead times for infrastructure in the new region; certification audits; and operations — on-call and support coverage across time zones.

Each risk gets a likelihood and impact rating, an owner, a mitigation and a trigger. Mitigation means retiring risk where possible: get the legal interpretation in writing early; decide vendor replacements in the first month; order capacity now. I would keep contingency in the schedule around the migration of shared services, review the register weekly with engineering, legal and security, and report the top five to sponsors monthly. If the legal interpretation changes, the data-flow inventory is what lets us re-plan quickly.

questions.title: Error spike mid-rollout
questions.prompt: You are halfway through a staged rollout of a new payments service when error rates jump in one region and some customers cannot pay. You are the TPM on the launch. Walk me through the first hour and the following week.
hints: Who leads the incident, and what is your role?
Stabilise first or diagnose first?
Who needs to hear what, and how often?
followups: Engineers want to keep debugging instead of rolling back. What do you do?
A large customer's CTO calls your CEO. How do you support that conversation?
What goes into the post-incident review?
criteria: Declares an incident and sets roles quickly.
Prioritises stabilising (pause rollout, roll back) over diagnosing.
Runs communication on a cadence to internal and customer audiences.
Tracks customer impact.
Runs a blameless review with owned actions and launch-process changes.
outline: Minute 0–5: declare incident, severity, incident lead, comms lead, scribe.
Stabilise: pause rollout; roll back the affected region if errors persist past a threshold.
Communicate: status every 30 minutes internally; customer-facing status page; support briefed.
Measure impact: failed payments, affected customers, duration.
After: blameless review; actions with owners; update rollout gates and rollback criteria.
questions.reference:
First five minutes: declare an incident with a severity level and make sure there is one incident lead (usually the on-call engineering lead), a communications lead and a scribe. As TPM I often take communications and coordination so engineers can focus.

Stabilise before diagnosing: pause the rollout everywhere, and roll back the affected region if errors do not drop quickly — payments failing is customer harm, and the rollback plan exists for this moment. If engineers want to keep debugging, I would ask the incident lead to decide against a pre-agreed threshold, not by feel.

Communication runs on a fixed cadence: internal updates every 30 minutes, a customer-facing status message, support briefed with what to say, and executives told impact, actions and the next update time. I would keep a running count of failed payments and affected customers for follow-up.

In the following week: a blameless review that asks why the issue reached customers and why detection or rollback took as long as it did; actions with owners and dates; and changes to the rollout — tighter error thresholds that stop it automatically, smaller first stages, and a rehearsed rollback.

questions.title: Two directors, one scope
questions.prompt: Two engineering directors disagree on the scope of your program's first release. One wants full feature parity with the old system; the other wants a minimal release in half the time. Neither will move, and the date is in the program charter. How do you resolve it?
hints: What does each director optimise for, and what are they afraid of?
Who has the authority to decide?
What evidence would settle the disagreement?
followups: The decider says 'you two work it out'. What now?
One director goes around you to the VP. How do you respond?
How do you make sure the decision sticks?
criteria: Understands each director's goal and fear.
Builds a fact base (usage data, risk, cost of each option).
Frames options, including middle paths.
Brings the decision to the right owner with a recommendation.
Documents the decision and dissent; keeps relationships intact.
outline: One-to-ones with each director: goals, fears, non-negotiables.
Facts: usage of old-system features; customer commitments; cost and risk of each scope.
Options: full parity; minimal; minimal plus the top-used features; phased parity with dates.
Decision meeting with the accountable leader; recommendation; decide by date.
Write down decision and dissent; communicate; track.
questions.reference:
I would meet each director separately to understand what they are protecting. The parity director is probably worried about customers losing features and support load; the minimal-release director about the date and risk. Both are reasonable.

Then I would build facts: which old-system features are actually used and by whom, which are contractually committed, and the time and risk of each scope option. Usually the data shows a middle path: a first release with the features most customers use, then the rest in dated phases.

I would present the options with this evidence in one meeting with the accountable leader — the person who owns the charter — and a recommendation, and ask for a decision by a set date. If told ‘work it out’, I would propose the middle option in writing to both directors with a deadline for objections, and escalate again if needed. If a director goes around me, I would make sure the VP has the same options document. The final decision and any dissent are recorded and shared, so it is not relitigated every week.
pitfalls: Deciding yourself when you lack authority.

questions.title: Two minutes with the CTO
questions.prompt: Your program is three weeks behind because a vendor's hardware arrived late. You have two minutes in the CTO's staff meeting. Give the update.
hints: What does the CTO need to know, and what do they need to decide?
Lead with the headline.
What are you already doing, and what help do you need?
followups: The CTO asks why this was not flagged earlier. Answer.
The CTO asks what it would take to recover the three weeks. Answer.
How would you write the same update by email?
criteria: Leads with status and impact.
States cause briefly without blame.
Presents recovery options and recommendation.
Makes a specific ask.
Gives the next checkpoint.
outline: Headline: three weeks late; new forecast date with confidence.
Cause: vendor delivery slip, in one sentence.
Impact: what depends on the date.
Options: recover part via parallel testing; overtime (not recommended); accept slip.
Ask: decision or help (e.g. vendor escalation).
Next update and trigger for earlier alert.
questions.reference:
“Headline: the storage program is three weeks behind; new launch forecast is 14 March, high confidence. Cause: the vendor delivered the hardware three weeks late. Impact: the analytics migration that depends on us also moves, unless we act.

We can recover about a week by running acceptance tests in parallel with installation in two data centres, at some risk of rework. Recovering all three weeks would need weekend work for a month, which I don’t recommend.

My recommendation: accept a two-week slip with parallel testing. I need two things: your agreement on the slip, and help escalating with the vendor’s leadership so the second shipment is not late. Next update in our weekly report; I’ll flag sooner if the second shipment date moves.”

(The date is illustrative.) On ‘why not flagged earlier’: answer honestly — when the signal first appeared and what has changed so vendor delivery risks reach the CTO earlier.
pitfalls: A long story before the headline.
Blaming the vendor without a plan.

questions.title: Debt now or four weeks later
questions.prompt: Half of the engineering team wants to ship with a quick data model and fix it later. The other half wants four more weeks to build it properly. You are the TPM. How do you get to a decision?
hints: What does 'fix it later' cost, and how likely is later to happen?
Is the decision reversible after launch?
Who decides — you, engineering, or product?
followups: The quick option requires a data migration next year. Does that change your view?
Leadership asks for your recommendation, not just a process. Give it.
How do you make sure the 'fix later' work actually happens?
criteria: Frames the decision and its deadline.
Compares options on cost, risk, reversibility and time.
Brings data (migration cost, user impact, opportunity cost).
Facilitates a decision by the right owner; gives a recommendation when asked.
Commits the follow-up work with dates if debt is accepted.
outline: Frame: decide by when, by whom.
Option A: quick model; cost of later migration, risk of data issues, reversibility.
Option B: four weeks; cost of delay (revenue, commitments).
Middle: build the stable interface properly, keep internals quick.
Decision record; if A, schedule and fund the fix now.
questions.reference:
I would frame it as a decision with a deadline and an owner — usually the engineering lead together with the product manager — and make the options comparable: the cost of four weeks’ delay (commitments, revenue, the team’s next project) versus the cost of the quick model (a future migration, its risk to customer data, and how likely ‘later’ really is).

The key question is reversibility. If the quick model leaks into public APIs or stored data that other teams build on, fixing it later means a migration under live traffic — expensive and risky. If it stays behind a stable interface, it can be replaced quietly. That often reveals a middle option: design the interface and data contracts properly now, and keep the internals simple.

If leadership asks for my recommendation, I give one with its reasons. If we accept the debt, the fix is scheduled and staffed now, with a date and an owner, and the decision is recorded so the team knows why it was made.
pitfalls: Accepting debt with no plan to repay.

questions.title: A program you turned around
questions.prompt: Tell me about a program that was in trouble when you took it over or that went off track while you led it. What did you do?
hints: How did you diagnose the problem?
What did you change first, and why that?
What was the result, honestly?
followups: What did you not fix, and why?
Who resisted, and how did you handle it?
What would you do in the first week next time?
criteria: Clear diagnosis based on evidence.
Prioritised actions.
Worked through people without authority.
Honest result.
Transferable lessons.
outline: Situation: the program and the trouble.
Diagnosis: what you looked at.
Actions: first, second, third.
Resistance and how you handled it.
Result with numbers.
What you learned.
questions.reference: A strong answer (a model of structure, not a script): “I took over a data-centre migration that had missed two milestones. In the first week I rebuilt the plan from each team’s actual throughput and found that one network dependency was blocking four teams. I got that team a dedicated review slot with the network architects and re-sequenced the others to unblocked work. I also replaced the weekly status meeting with a dependency review. We still launched five weeks late — not the original date — but the forecast I gave in week two held. I learned to rebuild the plan from evidence before promising anything.”
pitfalls: A heroic story with no diagnosis.

questions.title: Telling leaders the date was wrong
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you had to tell leadership that a date you had committed to was no longer realistic.
hints: When did you know, and when did you say it?
How did you present it?
What happened to trust afterwards?
followups: Did you wait too long?
How did leadership react?
What do you do now to avoid surprising leaders?
criteria: Raised it as soon as evidence was clear.
Came with a new forecast and options.
Took responsibility.
Maintained or rebuilt trust.
Changed practice to surface risk earlier.
outline: The commitment and its context.
The evidence that it was wrong.
How and when you communicated.
Options and decision.
Outcome and lesson.
questions.reference: A strong answer (a model of structure, not a script): “Six weeks before a launch, integration testing showed our error rates were three times the target. I knew within two days that the date was not realistic. I told my director the same week with a new forecast range, the cause, and two options: launch to internal users on the date or delay three weeks. They chose the internal launch. It was uncomfortable, but because I came early and with options, the director asked me to run the next program. Now I share forecast ranges from the start, so a change is an update, not a surprise.”
